title: Coder Workspaces: Overview
text:
Overview
Coder Workspaces are on-demand virtual machines with commonly used data science tools pre-installed. Anyone with a UCSB NetID can create a workspace to use for the duration of the academic quarter. Workspaces are deleted at the end of each quarter.
The service is managed by the Library DREAM Lab and uses computing resources provided by the College of Letters and Science IT (LSIT).
See our Getting Started Guide for a step-by-step introduction to creating and connecting to your first workspace.

title: Coder Workspaces: Overview
text:
Workspace Lifecycle

Workspaces shut down (stop) after four hours of inactivity.
You can manually stop a workspace by clicking the “Stop” button in Coder.
To start a stopped workspace, click the workspace’s “Start” button. It may take a couple of minutes to resume.
Deleting a workspace deletes all files on the workspace!
All workspaces will be deleted at the end of each academic quarter.

title: Coder Workspaces: Overview
text:
Policies

  !
  
    Backup Your Data
    Data is not backed up; users are responsible for their own backups. Please use GitHub, Google Drive (via Rclone), or download important files regularly.
  


Backup your data: Data is not backed up; users are responsible for their own backups.
Deletion: All workspaces are automatically deleted at the end of each quarter.
Limits: Users may create and use only one workspace at a time. Multiple active workspaces may be deleted without notice.
Maintenance: Workspaces may be inaccessible during scheduled maintenance windows (announced via email).
Inactivity: Workspaces stop automatically after four hours of inactivity to conserve resources. They can be resumed by clicking the “Start” button.
Software Installation: Users may install additional software using standard package managers.
Access by Staff: Workspaces may be accessed by staff in the Library or LSIT. Confidential or sensitive information should not be stored.

        Frequently Asked Questions
        
          Everything you need to know about Coder workspaces, hardware, policies, file transfers, and the AI Gateway.
        
      
    
    
      
      Search frequently asked questions
      
      
        Clear
      
    
  



  

  
    
      
        Category
        Accounts & Access
      
    
    
      
        
          
            Who can use DREAM Lab Cloud Services?
            
          
        
        
          Anyone with an active UCSB NetID (students, faculty, and staff) can create and use a Coder workspace for coursework, research, and data science projects.
        
      
      
        
          
            How do I sign in to Coder?
            
          
        
        
          Visit coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu, click 'UCSB Login', and authenticate using your UCSB Single Sign-On credentials via Google.
        
      
      
        
          
            How long does a workspace last?
            
          
        
        
          Workspaces are provided for the duration of the academic quarter. At the end of each quarter, all workspaces are automatically deleted. Be sure to export your code and files before the end of the quarter.
        
      
    
  

  
    
      
        Category
        Workspaces & Hardware
      
    
    
      
        
          
            What hardware resources does each workspace receive?
            
          
        
        
          Each workspace runs as an isolated virtual machine configured with 4 vCPUs, 16 GiB of RAM, a 64 GB persistent User Data Disk, and a 15 GB OS Disk.
        
      
      
        
          
            Why did my workspace stop running?
            
          
        
        
          Workspaces automatically shut down after four hours of inactivity to conserve shared campus compute resources. You can resume at any time by clicking the 'Start' button on the dashboard.
        
      
      
        
          
            How many workspaces can I have at once?
            
          
        
        
          Users may create and use only one active workspace at a time. Multiple active workspaces per user may be deleted without prior notice.
        
      
    
  

  
    
      
        Category
        Software & Environments
      
    
    
      
        
          
            What software is preinstalled in Coder?
            
          
        
        
          All workspaces come with Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Docker 29.8, Pixi package manager, R 4.6.1, Git, GitHub CLI (gh), jq, and uv/uvx. You can also enable RStudio Server, JupyterLab, and VS Code during creation.
        
      
      
        
          
            Can I install additional packages and tools?
            
          
        
        
          Yes. You have full sudo access to install system packages with 'sudo apt install <package>', Python environments with 'uv' or 'pixi', and R packages with 'install.packages()'. Packages in your home directory persist between stops and starts.
        
      
      
        
          
            Can I use desktop VS Code instead of the browser?
            
          
        
        
          Yes! Enable 'Visual Studio Code (Desktop)' when creating your workspace. Install the Coder extension in local VS Code, log in to coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu, and connect directly.
        
      
    
  

  
    
      
        Category
        Data, Files & Backups
      
    
    
      
        
          
            Are my files backed up automatically?
            
          
        
        
          No! Coder workspaces are not backed up. Users are responsible for backing up their own work. We recommend pushing your code to GitHub, mounting Google Drive with Rclone, or downloading copies regularly.
        
      
      
        
          
            How do I upload and download files?
            
          
        
        
          You can use the built-in web File Browser on your workspace dashboard, use Magic Wormhole (run 'uvx magic-wormhole send <file>'), or mount your Google Drive via Rclone.
        
      
      
        
          
            Will my files remain after I stop my workspace?
            
          
        
        
          Yes. Stopping a workspace releases active compute resources but preserves all files in your home directory (~). However, permanently deleting a workspace destroys all files.
        
      
    
  

  
    
      
        Category
        AI Gateway & Agents
      
    
    
      
        
          
            What is the DREAM Lab AI Gateway?
            
          
        
        
          An experimental service providing OpenAI-compatible API access to Google Gemini models (including gemini-4-argon and gemini-3.8-flash) hosted by campus cloud providers for coding assistants and research.
        
      
      
        
          
            Can I send sensitive research data to the AI Gateway?
            
          
        
        
          No. The DREAM Lab AI Gateway is NOT approved for data classified as P3 or P4 under UC protection levels. Never send restricted or personally identifiable data.
        
      
      
        
          
            How do I use OpenCode with campus models?
            
          
        
        
          OpenCode is preinstalled on your workspace. Run 'opencode', and use '/models' to select campus-hosted models through College IT (CIT) or the DREAM Lab AI Gateway.
        
      
    
  

  
    
      
        Category
        Support & Troubleshooting
      
    
    
      
        
          
            My workspace won't start or is stuck. What should I do?
            
          
        
        
          Wait 2–3 minutes and refresh your browser. If it is still stuck, stop the workspace and click Start again. If problems persist, email dreamlab@library.ucsb.edu.
        
      
      
        
          
            Where can I get one-on-one help?
            
          
        
        
          Email dreamlab@library.ucsb.edu, drop by the Library DREAM Lab, or join the UCSB Carpentry Slack for community and staff support.

title: Using AI Coding Agents
section: Why Use Coder for AI Coding Agents?
text:
Why Use Coder for AI Coding Agents?
Coder workspaces provide a relatively safe way to experiment with AI coding agents like OpenCode, Claude Code, or OpenAI Codex. These tools, which generate and also execute code, are powerful, but they come with significant risks such as prompt injection or unintended file modifications.
Because Coder workspaces are isolated virtual machines, the potential damage a rogue AI agent can cause is contained and cannot harm your personal laptop or campus network.

title: Using AI Coding Agents
text:
OpenCode
OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with a wide range of AI services and model providers. It is preinstalled on all Coder Workspaces.
To launch OpenCode, run opencode in your workspace terminal:
opencode



Interactive OpenCode command-line interface in Coder.



  i
  
    Switching Models in OpenCode
    Inside OpenCode, type /models to search and select a model from your preferred model provider.

title: Using AI Coding Agents
text:
Campus AI Gateways
By default, OpenCode offers default cloud services. For data privacy and university compliance, we recommend routing requests through campus gateways:

1. College IT (CIT) AI Gateway
The College IT AI Gateway provides on-premises Large Language Model access for UCSB staff and faculty; incidental student use is supported. All inference runs directly on CIT hardware, and prompts stay on campus.
In OpenCode, run /models and filter for “CIT”.


2. DREAM Lab AI Gateway
The DREAM Lab AI Gateway provides access to Google Gemini models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
To use it, generate a key at the API Key Manager (UCSB NetID login required).
Configure OpenCode using one of two methods:

Provide the key in the DREAM Lab LLM API Key field when creating your workspace.
Or export the environment variable manually before launching:

export DREAMLAB_LLM_KEY=sk-...
opencode
Then run /models inside OpenCode and filter for “DREAM Lab”:



Selecting DREAM Lab models inside OpenCode.

text:
University of California, Santa Barbara
    Launch Coder ↗

title: Marimo Notebooks
text:
Overview
Marimo is a modern Python notebook tool. Unlike Jupyter, Marimo notebooks are stored as plain Python files and automatically re-run dependent cells when a cell changes. Marimo has integrated AI chat and agent tools that can be configured to use models through the DREAM Lab AI Gateway.

title: Marimo Notebooks
text:
Creating the Workspace & Installing Marimo
Create a standard workspace at coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu. A default workspace is sufficient (no extra optional software required).
Once booted, open a Terminal from the dashboard and run:
# Create a project folder and set it as your working directory
mkdir my-project
cd my-project

# Create a Python virtual environment with uv
uv venv

# Install marimo in the environment
uv pip install marimo

# Run the marimo server
uv run marimo edit --no-token --headless

title: Marimo Notebooks
section: Running Marimo in the Background with tmux
text:
Running Marimo in the Background with tmux
To keep Marimo running after closing your terminal window, use tmux:
# Run in a persistent tmux session
cd ~/my-project
tmux new-session -d -s marimo 'uv run marimo edit --no-token --headless'
To stop the background server at any time:
tmux kill-session -t marimo

Accessing the Marimo Interface
With Marimo running, access the interface through the Ports menu on your workspace dashboard:



Click the port associated with the Marimo server.





Create a new reactive notebook directly in your project folder.

title: Marimo Notebooks
text:
Configuring Chat and AI Agents
Marimo features integrated AI code generation and assistant chat. You can connect it to models through the DREAM Lab AI Gateway using your personal API key.

1. Install AI Dependencies
Open User Settings (gear icon in the top right). Under Optional Dependencies, ensure AI features are installed, or click Install with uv.


2. Add a Custom AI Provider
Under the AI panel, go to AI Providers and click Add Provider:

Provider name: litellm_proxy
Base URL: https://litellm.dreamlab.ucsb.edu
API key: your personal AI Gateway key



3. Add a Model
In the AI Models tab, click + Add Model. Choose litellm_proxy as the provider, enter gemini-3-flash-preview, and click Add.



Add a custom model from the litellm_proxy provider.




4. Configure AI Features to Use the Model
In the AI Features tab, set Provider to custom and choose your model for Autocomplete, Chat, and Edit models.



Configure autocomplete and assistant models.




5. Confirm Chat Interface
Open the Chat and Agents UI from the notebook menu to begin prompting.



Marimo integrated AI chat assistant.

text:

title: Transferring files to/from your Workspace
text:
Three Ways to Transfer Files
There are several ways to upload and download files to a Coder Workspace:

Coder’s built-in File Browser: The most straightforward visual option.
Magic Wormhole: Fast and convenient for moving files or project folders between machines or workspaces.
Rclone: Connects your workspace directly to your UCSB Google Drive.

title: Transferring files to/from your Workspace
text:
Coder File Browser
The most convenient way to transfer files to/from a Coder Workspace is to use the built-in File Browser, accessible directly from the workspace dashboard.



Clicking the File Browser button opens a web management interface in a new window.


Clicking the File Browser button from the workspace dashboard opens the File Browser in a new tab or window. (Ensure popups are enabled in your browser settings).



File Browser interface for uploading, downloading, and editing files.

title: Transferring files to/from your Workspace
text:
Magic Wormhole
Magic Wormhole is a command-line utility that makes it easy to send files and directories directly between two machines using a short, one-time code. No accounts, cloud servers, or SSH keys required — just run a command on each machine and the transfer happens over an end-to-end encrypted channel.
You can use Magic Wormhole without installation by running it with uvx, which executes Python tools in temporary environments. uvx is installed on all Coder Workspaces by default.

Sending a file or directory:
uvx magic-wormhole send ./myfile.txt
# or for a directory:
uvx magic-wormhole send ./my-project
Magic Wormhole will print a short one-time code such as 7-guitarist-revenge. Use that code on the receiving machine:


Receiving a file or directory:
uvx magic-wormhole receive 7-guitarist-revenge

  i
  
    Single-Use Codes
    The code is single-use and expires as soon as the transfer completes or is cancelled. This is a quick and secure way to migrate projects between Coder workspaces!

title: Transferring files to/from your Workspace
text:
Rclone: Connecting to Google Drive
Rclone is a powerful file transfer tool that can mount your Google Drive to a local directory (such as ~/gdrive) in your workspace.

  ℹ
  
    Desktop VS Code Required for Auth
    Initial authorization requires connecting to your workspace using the VS Code Desktop application so that browser authorization tokens can be forwarded to Rclone. Once configured, VS Code Desktop is no longer needed.
  


Connect to your workspace using desktop VS Code (click the VS Code Desktop icon on the dashboard).
In VS Code, open a Terminal (View → Terminal or `Ctrl+``).
Verify Rclone is installed, or install it:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install rclone
Authorize read-only access to your Google Drive:
rclone config create gdrive drive scopes drive.readonly
(For full read-write permissions, omit scopes drive.readonly).
A web browser tab will open. Grant Rclone permission to access your Google Drive. Once finished, return to the VS Code terminal.
Create a mount point folder:
mkdir ~/gdrive
Mount Google Drive in the background:
rclone mount gdrive: ~/gdrive --daemon
Confirm that you can view files in your Drive:
ls ~/gdrive

To disconnect your Google Drive folder when done, run:
umount ~/gdrive
If umount reports a busy device, ensure no files are open and your terminal is not currently inside the ~/gdrive directory.

title: Getting Started with Coder Workspaces
text:
What to expect
Anyone with an active UCSB NetID can create an isolated cloud workspace running Ubuntu Linux with data science tools like Python, R, Docker, and Pixi pre-configured.

  Log in with UCSB Google Single Sign-On
  Boot an environment in 2-3 minutes
  Work in your browser or connect with your local desktop tools

title: Getting Started with Coder Workspaces
text:
Creating a Workspace

Visit https://coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu.
Click UCSB Login and log in using UCSB SSO (via Google).
Click the New Workspace button.
On the New Workspace page:

Give the workspace a name (required).
Check I understand the usage policies (required).
Select additional software and workspace options to enable (see below).
Click Create Workspace.

It may take a couple of minutes for the workspace to boot.


New Workspace Options
When creating a workspace, you can configure:

RStudio: Enables the RStudio Server system service on port 8787.
JupyterLab: Installs JupyterLab and commonly used packages (pip, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, ipython, and jupyter-ai) into a global Pixi environment (coder-jupyter). Runs in the background on port 19999 with ~/workspace as the working directory.
Visual Studio Code (Desktop): Configures the Coder agent to enable desktop VS Code support, surfacing direct connection buttons to launch remote sessions.
Visual Studio Code (Web): Deploys the browser-based vscode-web service rooted at /home/coder/workspace.
DREAM Lab LLM API Key: Injects your DREAM Lab AI Gateway key into the workspace as $DREAMLAB_LLM_KEY for automated OpenCode authentication.

title: Getting Started with Coder Workspaces
text:
Connecting to Your Workspace
Once your workspace is created, you will be directed to the workspace dashboard. You can interact with your workspace directly through the browser or via software on your local machine.



Workspace dashboard with buttons for web-based IDEs and terminal.



Browser-Based Tools

JupyterLab or RStudio: Web-based IDEs for data analysis in Python or R.
File Browser: For navigating your workspace’s file system and transferring files.
Terminal: A browser-based terminal that provides instant access to your workspace shell environment.

To use these, simply click the corresponding icon on your workspace’s dashboard page.

title: Getting Started with Coder Workspaces
text:
Connecting with Locally Installed Software
For a more integrated development experience, connect your local editor or terminal to your Coder workspace.

Connecting via Desktop VS Code

Ensure you have the Visual Studio Code desktop application installed.
Install the official Coder extension from the VS Code Marketplace.
Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) and run: Coder: Login
Enter your Coder deployment URL: https://coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu
After logging in, browse your workspaces in the Coder view on the sidebar, or run Coder: Open Workspace.



Connecting via Coder CLI
The Coder CLI allows authenticating and connecting to workspaces directly from your terminal.
Installing the Coder CLI (macOS / Linux):
curl -L https://coder.com/install.sh | sh
For Windows, download and run the installer executable from Coder’s GitHub Releases page.
Authenticate the CLI:
coder login https://coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu
Follow the prompts to complete authentication in your browser.
Connecting via SSH:
coder ssh <workspace-name>

  i
  
    Persistence & Lifecycle
    Files stored in your home directory persist when you stop and restart your workspace. Remember that workspaces auto-stop after 4 hours of inactivity and are deleted at the end of each academic quarter.

title: Getting Started with RStudio
text:
Overview
RStudio is a powerful integrated development environment (IDE) for R programming. Coder workspaces allow you to run RStudio Server, which provides the full RStudio interface accessible securely through any modern web browser.

title: Getting Started with RStudio
text:
Creating a Workspace with RStudio

  ℹ
  
    Enable during creation
    RStudio must be enabled when the workspace is created. It cannot be added to an existing workspace after creation.
  


Navigate to the New Workspace page at coder.dreamlab.ucsb.edu.
Complete the required workspace name and policy checks.
Make sure Include RStudio is set to Yes.
Click Create Workspace.

Once booted, launch RStudio in a new browser tab with the RStudio button on the dashboard:



Coder workspace dashboard showing RStudio button on port 8787.

title: Getting Started with RStudio
text:
Setting Up an RStudio Project
RStudio Projects organize your scripts, datasets, and working directories cleanly:

In RStudio, click File → New Project.
Select New Directory.
Choose New Project.
Enter a directory name (e.g., my-project) and keep the parent directory set to ~.
Click Create Project.

RStudio generates an .Rproj file storing project-specific settings so you can easily resume work.

title: Getting Started with RStudio
text:
Installing Packages & Git Setup
Install packages in your cloud RStudio session just like a local installation:
# Install from CRAN
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("ggplot2")

# Install from GitHub
install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("username/repository")

  i
  
    Isolated Package Storage
    Packages installed in your workspace persist across sessions within your persistent home directory, isolated from other workspaces to ensure reproducibility.
  


Setting Up Git
Open the Terminal in RStudio (Tools → Terminal → New Terminal) and configure your identity:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"


Additional Resources

RStudio User Guide ↗ — Comprehensive documentation.
RStudio Cheat Sheets ↗ — Quick syntax and workflow reference.
R for Data Science (2e) ↗ — Definitive guide to modern data science in R.
Posit Community ↗ — Knowledge sharing and Q&A.

title: Using the UCSB AI Commons API
text:
Overview & Prerequisites
This walkthrough explains how to configure the UCSB AI Commons API for two tools:

OpenCode (terminal-based coding agent)
Continue (VS Code and Positron extension)


  !
  
    Requesting API Access
    The API is an add-on feature to AI Commons. To request access, submit your request in Service-Now. Once approved, you will see API Key in your My Menu portal list.
  




AI Commons portal navigation with API Key option.





AI Commons API dashboard interface.



Querying Model Names
To list the models enabled on your account, run:
curl -s https://YOUR-AI-COMMONS-ENDPOINT/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_AI_COMMONS_API_KEY" \
  | python -c "import sys, json; [print(m['id']) for m in json.load(sys.stdin)['data']]"

title: Using the UCSB AI Commons API
Using the UCSB AI Commons API
text:
Configuring Continue (VS Code / Positron)

Search for and install Continue from the VS Code Extensions Marketplace.
Open the Continue panel, click the gear icon (Settings), select Configs, and open Main Config (~/.continue/config.yaml).




Opening Main Config in Continue extension.



Configuration YAML
name: UCSB AI Commons
version: 1.0.0
schema: v1

models:
  - name: Claude Sonnet 4.6
    provider: openai
    model: claude-v4.6-sonnet
    apiBase: https://YOUR-AI-COMMONS-ENDPOINT/v1
    apiKey: YOUR_AI_COMMONS_API_KEY
    roles:
      - chat
      - edit
    capabilities:
      - tool_use

  - name: Claude Opus 4.6
    provider: openai
    model: claude-v4.6-opus
    apiBase: https://YOUR-AI-COMMONS-ENDPOINT/v1
    apiKey: YOUR_AI_COMMONS_API_KEY
    roles:
      - chat
      - edit
    capabilities:
      - tool_use

  - name: Claude Haiku 4.5
    provider: openai
    model: claude-v4.5-haiku
    apiBase: https://YOUR-AI-COMMONS-ENDPOINT/v1
    apiKey: YOUR_AI_COMMONS_API_KEY
    roles:
      - chat
      - edit
    capabilities:
      - tool_use
Replace the endpoint URL and API key with your values, then open the Continue panel to start coding with your models.

title: Using the UCSB AI Commons API
text:
Authentication Troubleshooting

Verify your Base URL is correct.
Confirm /v1 is not duplicated (e.g. avoid /v1/v1).
Confirm the API key is active in the AI Commons portal.
Ensure no leading or trailing whitespace was copied.

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
University of California, Santa Barbara

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
Overview
DREAM Lab’s AI gateway service provides API access to Large Language Models (LLMs) hosted by campus cloud providers (currently, Google). It can be used in conjunction with a coding agent (such as OpenCode or Continue) or to build custom research AI workflows.
Note: The gateway does not provide a web chat UI. The service is primarily oriented toward DREAM Lab workshop attendees, researchers learning AI-assisted coding, and Library staff.

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
API Endpoint & Supported Models
The OpenAI-compatible API endpoint for the gateway service is:
https://litellm.dreamlab.ucsb.edu/v1

Supported Google Gemini Models








Model Name
Best For
Description




gemini-4-argon
Complex reasoning & coding
Frontier model for challenging reasoning and software architecture tasks.


gemini-3.8-flash
Agentic coding
Fast, highly capable model tuned for autonomous agent execution loops.


gemini-3.5-flash-lite
Low-cost inference
High-throughput model ideal for text processing and lightweight tasks.


gemini-embedding-2
Embeddings
Multimodal embedding model for vector search and retrieval.

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
Creating an API Key
Anyone with a valid UCSB NetID can create a key through the API Key Manager ↗.

  ℹ
  
    Key Policies & Restrictions
    
      
        You may have only one active key at a time.
        If you regenerate a new key, your previous key is automatically disabled.
        Keys expire automatically after three months.
        Your key has an allocated budget that resets periodically. Use the key manager to view your remaining balance.
        Usage reflects real API expenses; requests to larger models consume quota faster than lighter models.

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
Using the Gateway with Python
Because the gateway exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, you can interact with models using the standard openai Python library:
mkdir llm-example
cd llm-example
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install openai
Create a script (main.py) specifying the gateway base URL:
import os
from openai import OpenAI

# In a Coder Workspace with a configured key, DREAMLAB_LLM_KEY is set automatically
api_key = os.environ.get("DREAMLAB_LLM_KEY", "your-api-key-here")

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=api_key,
    base_url="https://litellm.dreamlab.ucsb.edu/v1"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gemini-3.5-flash-lite",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Explain the difference between a list and a tuple in Python."}
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
Run the script:
python main.py

title: DREAM Lab AI Gateway
text:
Data Privacy & Security

  !
  
    Data Classification Restriction
    The DREAM Lab AI Gateway IS NOT approved for use with data classified as P3 or P4 under the UC data protection levels.
  

The service routes requests through Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Google will not use campus data to train or fine-tune AI models. For full compliance details, see UC Protection Levels and Google’s zero data retention agreements.
